Dagon
DAY-gon
proper noun (a national god of the Philistines)
Hebrew Dagon, most likely from dagan, grain (H1715), pointing to an original character as a god of agriculture and the harvest among the Canaanite and Philistine peoples; later Jewish tradition also connected the name to dag, fish (H1709), on the strength of the ruin left of him in 1 Samuel 5:4.

Biblical Definition

Dagon was the national god of the Philistines, with temples at Ashdod and Gaza. When the Philistines captured the ark of God in battle, they carried it in triumph into the house of Dagon at Ashdod and set it beside him, as though the LORD were merely one captive god placed alongside another. The LORD answered the insult directly: on the first morning Dagon was found fallen on his face to the ground before the ark; set upright again, he was found the second morning fallen once more, this time with his head and both palms broken off, only the stump of him left. So notorious was the ruin that the Philistines’ own priests refused ever after to tread on the threshold of Dagon’s house at Ashdod (1Sa 5:5). Later, after Saul’s death on Gilboa, the Philistines fastened his head in the temple of Dagon and hung his armor in the house of their gods (1Ch 10:10); earlier still, Samson had been brought out to entertain the Philistine lords at a great sacrifice to Dagon, and pulled the temple down upon them in his death (Jdg 16:23-30). Every appearance of Dagon in Scripture ends the same way: a carved thing that cannot stand upright before the ark of the living God, and cannot save the men who trust it.

Webster 1828 Definition

The chief idol-god of the Philistines, worshipped at Ashdod and Gaza, twice cast down before the ark of the LORD.

expand to see more

DAGON, n. The national idol-god of the Philistines, worshipped at Ashdod, Gaza, and elsewhere.

His temple at Ashdod received the captured ark of the LORD, set beside him as a captive trophy.

The image was found fallen before the ark, and afterward fallen a second time with head and hands broken off.

His priests thereafter would not tread on the threshold of his house.

Saul’s head was later fastened in Dagon’s temple after the defeat at Gilboa.

Key Scripture

Jdg 16:23 — "Then the lords of the Philistines gathered them together for to offer a great sacrifice unto Dagon their god, and to rejoice: for they said, Our god hath delivered Samson our enemy into our hand."

1Sa 5:2 — "When the Philistines took the ark of God, they brought it into the house of Dagon, and set it by Dagon."

1Sa 5:5 — "Therefore neither the priests of Dagon, nor any that come into Dagon's house, tread on the threshold of Dagon in Ashdod unto this day."

1Ch 10:10 — "And they put his armour in the house of their gods, and fastened his head in the temple of Dagon."

Modern Corruption

No one burns incense to a literal fish-idol named Dagon today, so the word reads as pure antiquity; the principle it fixes — that whatever is enthroned beside the ark will not stand — is not antique at all.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Nothing in the modern world worships Dagon by name, and the word carries none of the live theological battle that surrounds terms like grace or justice.

The principle to recover is what the two mornings in Ashdod actually establish: a false god does not merely fail to help; set beside the true and living God, it is broken. The Philistines meant the ark’s placement in Dagon’s house as a trophy of their god’s supremacy, and the LORD answered not with argument but with a wrecked statue on its own threshold. Every generation builds its own house of Dagon — some ultimate thing, project, or ideology set up as the thing that finally secures a people’s life and future — and every generation is offered the same lesson the Ashdodites received twice: what is not the LORD, set beside the LORD, will be found face down.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew dagan (H1715), grain, the likely root of Dagon’s name and character as a harvest-god of the Philistines; later folk tradition read it instead by dag, fish.

expand to see more

Hebrew dagan (H1715) — corn, grain; the probable root, marking Dagon as an agricultural, harvest deity.

Hebrew dag (H1709) — fish; a later folk-etymology suggested by the “stump” left of the idol in 1 Samuel 5:4.

Hebrew beyth Dagon — house of Dagon, the temple name at Ashdod, distinct from the place-name Beth-dagon elsewhere in Judah and Asher.

Hebrew aron (H727) — the ark, the object set beside Dagon and the instrument of his ruin.

Hebrew miphtan (H4670) — threshold; the very spot on which Dagon’s head and hands were found, and which his priests would not afterward tread.

Usage

"“Dagon was fallen upon his face to the ground before the ark of the LORD” — the first morning in Ashdod."

"“The priests of Dagon... tread not on the threshold” — the custom his ruin produced."

"“They... fastened his head in the temple of Dagon” — the same house, a different captive, after Gilboa."
